dublinCore.title: Nyquist-Shannon Sampling
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Sampling
Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem
Nyquist rate
Aliasing
Signal reconstruction
dublinCore.description: A 5 Hz sine wave is sampled at a rate set by one slider (1 to 50 Hz). The upper plot shows the original wave and its samples; the lower plot rebuilds the signal from the samples by ideal sinc interpolation and by straight lines, and a status line reports whether the rate is above the 10 Hz Nyquist rate and gives the alias frequency when it is not.

learningObjectives: State the Nyquist criterion fs > 2f and calculate the Nyquist rate of a sinusoid of known frequency
Calculate the samples per period fs/f and the Nyquist frequency fs/2 for a given sampling rate
Predict the alias frequency fa = |f - k fs| when fs < 2f and verify it by counting the cycles of the reconstruction
Distinguish ideal (sinc) reconstruction from straight-line interpolation and explain why a jagged straight-line plot does not mean that information was lost
Explain why sampling at exactly fs = 2f can fail to capture a sine wave
prerequisites: Frequency and period of a sine wave
Sampling as x[n] = x(n Ts) with Ts = 1/fs

misconceptions.misconception: A sine wave needs many samples per period, such as ten, to be captured
misconceptions.correction: Any rate above 2f determines the sine wave; ideal sinc reconstruction recovers it even when straight lines between the samples look badly distorted
misconceptions.evidence: At fs = 12 Hz (2.4 samples per period) the gray straight-line curve zigzags while the blue sinc curve matches the 5 Hz original

misconceptions.misconception: Sampling at exactly twice the signal frequency is enough
misconceptions.correction: The criterion is the strict inequality fs > 2f; at exactly 2f the samples can all land on zero crossings
misconceptions.evidence: At fs = 10.0 Hz every sample is zero and both reconstructions are flat lines

misconceptions.misconception: Aliasing makes a signal look noisy or distorted
misconceptions.correction: An aliased sinusoid reconstructs as a clean sinusoid at the wrong, lower frequency
misconceptions.evidence: At fs = 8.0 Hz the blue curve is a smooth 3 Hz sine wave instead of the 5 Hz original

accessibility.screenReaderScript: A 5 hertz sine wave is sampled at the rate set by one slider, from 1 to 50 samples per second. The upper plot shows the original wave with its samples. The lower plot shows the ideal sinc reconstruction and a straight-line reconstruction. A status line says whether the rate is above the 10 hertz Nyquist rate and gives the alias frequency when it is not.

controls.label: Sampling rate fs (Hz)
controls.description: Sets the sampling rate in samples per second; the read-out also gives fs/5, the number of samples per period of the 5 Hz signal

visualElements.description: Upper plot: the original 5 Hz sine wave in black with its samples as red dots over a one-second window
Lower plot: the ideal sinc reconstruction in blue and the straight-line reconstruction in gray, both drawn through the red samples, with a legend and a time axis in seconds
Read-out of f, the Nyquist rate 2f, the Nyquist frequency fs/2 and samples per period, plus a colored Nyquist status line that gives the alias frequency when fs < 2f

model.description: Samples x(t) = sin(2 pi 5 t) at t = n / fs and rebuilds a continuous signal by Whittaker-Shannon (sinc) interpolation and by linear interpolation; the alias frequency is found by folding f into [0, fs/2]
equations: x[n] = sin(2 pi f n / fs)
x_r(t) = sum_n x[n] sinc(fs t - n)
fa = |f - k fs|, with integer k chosen so that fa <= fs / 2
algorithms: Truncated sinc sum over the samples in the window plus 2000 samples beyond each edge, recomputed only when fs or the canvas width changes

instructionalStrategies: Predict the alias frequency, then verify with the slider
Locate the Nyquist rate by approaching 10 Hz from above and below
extensions: Explore spectral replication and reconstruction filters in the Sampling Theorem Explorer
Add a phase slider to show that sampling at exactly 2f gives samples whose size depends on the phase
